The best chain on garnet right now is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I read the current default calibration of the real garnet QPU (calibration set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). It lists 28 calibrated CZ pairs, and every pair has an interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) fidelity. I checked every chain of 3 qubits that is joined by two CZ pairs. QB7-QB12 has a CZ fidelity of 0.998016. QB12-QB11 has 0.998693. Their product is 0.996712, which is the highest of all chains. The second-best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16 at 0.994689.

Next I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB7, QB12 and QB11. A rotation put QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Then two CNOTs copied QB12 onto QB7 and onto QB11. I built each CNOT from native rotations around one CZ gate. The only CZ gates were on QB12-QB7 and QB12-QB11. Then I measured all 3 qubits in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots, as job 01a1603f-935f-765e-ad1d-7dfeeb719b8f. The job completed. The counts were 000: 48, 001: 50, 110: 47, 111: 55.

A perfect quantum computer would give only 000 and 111, about half each. That is the GHZ principle. The 3 qubits are entangled, so measuring them always gives the same value on all 3, even though each single qubit is random. The mock counts include 001 and 110. They do not mean the circuit is wrong. The garnet:mock service does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bitstrings to test that a job is accepted and runs. Mock jobs cost 0 credits. To see real GHZ correlations, run the same circuit on the real garnet QPU. That run would cost credits.
